concepts.name: Prime factorisation
concepts.description: Every number breaks into primes in exactly one way; that fingerprint answers most factor questions.

concepts.name: Counting and summing factors
concepts.description: Add one to each exponent and multiply to count; use geometric sums to add.

concepts.name: Counting multiples
concepts.description: Multiples of k up to n number ⌊n ÷ k⌋; combine sets with inclusion–exclusion.

concepts.name: Perfect squares
concepts.description: A number is a perfect square exactly when every prime exponent is even.

formulas.title: Prime factorisation
formulas.prompt: How do you write a number in prime-factor form?
formulas.explanation: Divide out the smallest prime again and again until only primes remain, then collect equal primes into powers.
formulas.commonMistake: Stopping at a composite factor such as 60 = 2 × 30.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Write 84 as a product of prime powers.

formulas.title: Number of factors
formulas.prompt: If N = p^a × q^b × r^c, how many factors does N have?
formulas.explanation: A factor picks an exponent from 0 to a for p, 0 to b for q, and so on. The choices multiply.

formulas.title: Sum of factors
formulas.prompt: If N = p^a × q^b, what is the sum of all its factors?
formulas.explanation: Expanding this product produces every factor exactly once.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the sum of all factors of 12.

formulas.title: Counting multiples
formulas.prompt: How many multiples of k are there from 1 to n?
formulas.formula:
Count = ⌊n ÷ k⌋
A or B: ⌊n/a⌋ + ⌊n/b⌋ − ⌊n/LCM(a, b)⌋
formulas.explanation: Divide and drop the remainder. When counting numbers divisible by a or b, the common multiples were counted twice, so subtract them once.
formulas.commonMistake: Rounding up, or forgetting to subtract the overlap.
formulas.applicationPrompt: How many multiples of 6 are there between 1 and 100?

formulas.title: Perfect squares
formulas.prompt: When is a number a perfect square, and how many factors does it have?
formulas.formula: Perfect square ⇔ every exponent is even ⇔ odd number of factors
formulas.explanation: Factors come in pairs (d, N ÷ d), except when d = √N. Only squares have that unpaired factor.
formulas.commonMistake: Multiplying by every odd-exponent prime twice.
formulas.applicationPrompt: What is the smallest number that 180 must be multiplied by to give a perfect square?

formulas.title: Odd and even factors
formulas.prompt: How many factors of a number are odd, and how many even?
formulas.formula:
Odd factors: count the factors of the odd part (ignore the 2s)
Even factors = all factors − odd factors
formulas.explanation: An odd factor cannot contain 2, so the power of 2 must be 0.
formulas.example: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5: odd factors (2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 6, all factors 24, so 18 even.
formulas.commonMistake: Halving the total number of factors.
formulas.applicationPrompt: How many even factors does 720 have?

formulas.title: Factors that are perfect squares
formulas.prompt: How many factors of N are perfect squares?
formulas.formula:
For each prime power pᵉ, choose an even exponent: ⌊e/2⌋ + 1 ways
Multiply the choices
formulas.explanation: A square factor uses only even powers of each prime.
formulas.commonMistake: Counting the odd exponents as well.
formulas.applicationPrompt: How many factors of 2⁴ × 3⁵ × 7² are perfect squares?

levels.title: The Prime Fingerprint
levels.description: Break a number into primes once and every factor question becomes counting.

blocks.title: One way to build every number
blocks.body: Every whole number above 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way. 60 = 2² × 3 × 5, and no other combination of primes gives 60. That uniqueness is what makes prime factorisation so powerful.

blocks.title: Counting factors
blocks.body:
N = pᵃ × qᵇ × rᶜ
Number of factors = (a + 1)(b + 1)(c + 1)
blocks.caption: A factor may use each prime any number of times from 0 up to its exponent.

blocks.title: Multiples go the other way
blocks.body: The multiples of k up to n number ⌊n ÷ k⌋. To count numbers divisible by a or b, add the two counts and subtract the multiples of LCM(a, b), which were counted twice.

levels.title: Factors Formulas
levels.description: Factorisation, factor counts, sums, multiples and squares.

levels.title: Counting with Restrictions
levels.description: Sums, odd factors, overlaps and squares.

levels.title: Structured Factor Problems
levels.description: Restricted exponent ranges and square factors.

questions.question: Which of these is the prime factorisation of 60?
questions.explanation: 60 = 2 × 30 = 2 × 2 × 15 = 2² × 3 × 5. The others either contain a composite (10, 4) or multiply to a different number (90).
questions.method: Keep dividing by primes until all factors are prime.

hints.text: Every factor in the answer must itself be prime.
Two of the options contain a composite number.

commonMistakes: Leaving a composite such as 10 or 4 in the factorisation.

questions.question: How many factors does 36 have?
questions.method: Add 1 to each exponent and multiply.

hints.text: Start with the prime factorisation.
Add one to each exponent.

questions.question: How many multiples of 7 are there from 1 to 100?
questions.explanation: ⌊100 ÷ 7⌋ = 14, because 7 × 14 = 98 is the last multiple not above 100.

hints.text: What is the largest multiple of 7 that does not exceed 100?

questions.question: If N = pᵃ × qᵇ (p and q distinct primes), the number of factors of N is
questions.explanation: A factor uses p to some power from 0 to a (a + 1 choices) and q to some power from 0 to b (b + 1 choices). The choices multiply.
questions.method: Count the choices for each prime and multiply.

hints.text: A factor may use p zero times, so p has more than a choices.

questions.question: Which of these numbers is prime?
questions.explanation: 51 = 3 × 17, 57 = 3 × 19 and 91 = 7 × 13. Only 59 has no factor other than 1 and itself.
questions.method: Test divisibility by primes up to the square root.

hints.text: Numbers that look prime often hide a factor of 3 or 7.
Check the digit sum for 3.

commonMistakes: Treating 51, 57 or 91 as prime because they look odd and irregular.

questions.question: How many factors does 72 have?
questions.method: Prime-factorise, add 1 to each exponent, multiply.

hints.text: Factorise 72 completely first.

questions.question: What is the sum of all the factors of 28?
questions.method: Multiply the geometric sums for each prime.

hints.text: List the powers of each prime from 0 up to its exponent.
Multiply the two sums.

questions.question: How many odd factors does 360 have?
questions.explanation: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5. An odd factor cannot use any 2, so the exponent of 2 is fixed at 0: (2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 6.
questions.method: Set the exponent of 2 to zero and count the rest.

hints.text: Which prime makes a factor even?
Remove it from the count.

commonMistakes: Giving 24, the count of all factors.

questions.question: How many numbers from 1 to 100 are divisible by 4 or 6?
questions.explanation: Multiples of 4: 25. Multiples of 6: 16. Multiples of both are multiples of 12: 8. Total = 25 + 16 − 8 = 33.

hints.text: Some numbers are multiples of both 4 and 6 and got counted twice.
Both means a multiple of 12, not 24.

commonMistakes: Not subtracting the overlap (41) or using 4 × 6 = 24 for the overlap.

questions.question: What is the smallest number by which 180 must be multiplied to make it a perfect square?
questions.explanation: 180 = 2² × 3² × 5. Only the 5 has an odd exponent, so one more 5 makes every exponent even: 180 × 5 = 900 = 30².
questions.method: Multiply by the primes whose exponents are odd.

hints.text: Write 180 in prime powers.
Which prime is unpaired?

commonMistakes: Multiplying by 6 or 2, which changes the wrong exponents.

questions.question: How many factors of 2⁴ × 3³ × 5² are multiples of 6?
questions.explanation: A multiple of 6 needs at least one 2 and one 3. Exponent of 2: 1 to 4 (4 choices); of 3: 1 to 3 (3 choices); of 5: 0 to 2 (3 choices). 4 × 3 × 3 = 36.
questions.method: Restrict the exponent range for each prime, then multiply.

hints.text: What must every multiple of 6 contain?
Count the allowed exponents for each prime separately.

questions.question: How many factors of 720 are perfect squares?
questions.explanation: 720 = 2⁴ × 3² × 5. A square factor needs even exponents: 2 can use 0, 2, 4 (3 choices), 3 can use 0, 2 (2 choices), 5 must use 0 (1 choice). 3 × 2 × 1 = 6.
questions.method: Count only the even exponents for each prime.

hints.text: A perfect square has only even exponents.
Count the even exponents available to each prime.

questions.question: Which of these numbers has exactly 3 factors?
questions.explanation: Exactly three factors means the form p². 49 = 7² has factors 1, 7, 49. 36 has 9, 50 has 6 and 64 has 7.
solutionSteps: (a + 1) = 3 gives a = 2 for a single prime.
So the number is the square of a prime.
questions.method: Three factors ⇒ the square of a prime.

hints.text: Three is prime, so only one prime can be present.

commonMistakes: Choosing any perfect square such as 36 or 64.
